content: A nucleic acid is a large macromolecule made up of chains of nucleotides. In biochemistry, these molecules are responsible for carrying genetic information or forming structural components within cells. The two most common types of nucleic acids are deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA). Nucleic acids are universally present in all living organisms, as they are found in every cell, and they are also present in viruses. Synthetic nucleic acids, such as peptide nucleic acid (PNA), Morpholino, locked nucleic acid (LNA), glycol nucleic acid (GNA), and threose nucleic acid (TNA), differ from natural DNA and RNA due to modifications in their molecular backbones. The term nucleic acid refers to a family of biopolymers that are named for their association with the cell nucleus. Nucleic acids are composed of monomers called nucleotides. Each nucleotide consists of three components: a nitrogenous base (either a purine or a pyrimidine), a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group. The sugar component differs between DNA and RNA; DNA contains 2-deoxyribose, while RNA contains ribose. The nitrogenous bases also vary between the two: adenine, cytosine, and guanine are found in both DNA and RNA, but thymine is exclusive to DNA, and uracil is exclusive to RNA. Rare bases, such as inosine, can also occur, particularly in mature transfer RNA (tRNA). Nucleic acids can exist as single-stranded or double-stranded molecules, though more complex structures with three or more strands can also form. Double-stranded nucleic acids, such as the DNA double helix, are stabilized by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. In contrast, RNA is typically single-stranded but can fold into secondary structures, such as those seen in tRNA and ribosomal RNA (rRNA). In cells, DNA is predominantly double-stranded, although some viruses have single-stranded DNA genomes. Retroviruses, on the other hand, have single-stranded RNA genomes. The sugar and phosphate groups in nucleic acids are linked in an alternating chain, forming a phosphodiester bond. This arrangement gives nucleic acids a directionality, with distinct 3' and 5' ends based on the carbons of the sugar molecule. The nitrogenous bases are attached to the 1' carbon of the sugar via a glycosidic bond, with pyrimidines linked through their N-1 atom and purines through their N-9 atom. Ribonucleic acid (RNA) is a polymer of nucleotides that plays critical roles in translating genetic information from DNA into proteins. RNA serves as a messenger (mRNA) between DNA and ribosomes, forms essential components of ribosomes (rRNA), and acts as a carrier molecule (tRNA) for amino acids during protein synthesis. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is a nucleic acid that stores the genetic instructions necessary for the development and functioning of all known living organisms. DNA is often compared to a blueprint, as it contains the information required to construct cellular components, including proteins and RNA molecules. Segments of DNA that encode genetic information are called genes, while other DNA sequences serve structural or regulatory functions. Nucleobases are nitrogen-containing heterocyclic aromatic compounds that participate in base pairing within DNA and RNA. The primary nucleobases are cytosine, guanine, adenine, thymine (in DNA), and uracil (in RNA). These bases are abbreviated as C, G, A, T, and U, respectively. Base pairing is complementary: cytosine pairs with guanine, and adenine pairs with thymine in DNA or uracil in RNA. The cytosine-guanine pair is more stable than the adenine-thymine pair due to the presence of three hydrogen bonds versus two. DNA molecules with higher guanine-cytosine content are more thermally stable. Nucleobases are classified into two groups: purines (adenine and guanine) with a double-ring structure, and pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, and uracil) with a single-ring structure. Mutant forms of purines, such as hypoxanthine and xanthine, can arise through processes like deamination. Nucleosides are molecules formed by attaching a nucleobase to a sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) via a glycosidic bond. Common nucleosides include cytidine, uridine, adenosine, guanosine, and thymidine. When a phosphate group is added to a nucleoside, it becomes a nucleotide. Nucleoside analogs, such as acyclovir, are used as antiviral drugs. Nucleotides consist of a nucleoside and one or more phosphate groups. They are the building blocks of RNA and DNA and also serve as structural components of important cofactors, such as coenzyme A (CoA), flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), flavin mononucleotide (FMN), adenosine triphosphate (ATP), and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP). Nucleotides play essential roles in cellular metabolism and signaling. They are named based on their nucleoside and the number of phosphate groups they contain. For example, adenine linked to ribose forms the nucleoside adenosine, which becomes adenosine monophosphate (AMP) when bonded to a single phosphate group. Additional phosphates result in adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP).
